metaTitle: Agricultural Solar in California: 2026 Farm Guide
metaDescription: California farm solar guide for 2026: PG&E AG-rate schedules, NEM aggregation across meters, and why USDA REAP grants are paused as of Sept 2026.
h1: Solar for California Farms and Agricultural Operations
intro:
USDA REAP grants have not accepted a new application since April 1, 2026. USDA rescinded the prior funding notice to comply with a federal executive order targeting renewable energy subsidies, and as of today, September 5, 2026, no replacement funding opportunity has been published. If your farm solar plan assumed a REAP grant covering a quarter to half of project cost, that assumption needs to change before you sign anything. The one door still open: REAP guaranteed loans, accepted year-round through local USDA Rural Development offices.

That's the headline. The rest of the picture is more workable. PG&E's agricultural rate schedules charge up to $0.22830/kWh for summer peak generation on AG-B, and irrigation pumps that run through July and August are exactly the load that peak pricing punishes. Net Energy Metering Aggregation lets one array offset a home meter and every pump meter on contiguous land, which is the only reason ag solar sizes sensibly against seasonal load instead of requiring a standalone system at every wellhead.

This page covers PG&E and SCE ag rate structures, meter aggregation, what's actually confirmed about REAP and pending state legislation, and where the cost data runs thin. We flag every number we couldn't independently verify — there's more of that than usual on this page, because ag-specific data is harder to pin down than residential rates.

sections.heading: Irrigation Load Doesn't Behave Like a Rooftop Load
sections.body:
A house draws power fairly evenly across the year. A pump doesn't. Central Valley irrigation runs hard from roughly April through September and drops to near-zero the rest of the year, which is a terrible match for a standalone solar system sized against that one meter's usage — you'd be paying off a system that sits mostly idle five or six months a year.

The fix isn't a bigger array at the pump. It's combining the pump's seasonal peak-season draw with steadier year-round load elsewhere on the operation — a home, a packing shed, an office meter — so the system has something to offset in the off-season too. That's the entire logic behind meter aggregation, covered in detail below, and it's the first question a farm should answer before sizing anything: how many meters, on what parcels, with what load profile, can legally be combined onto one interconnection.

The other structural fact worth knowing going in: California's agricultural water use is under real pressure from the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, and research by EPIC scholars at the University of Chicago finds California farmers are roughly ten times more price-responsive to electricity costs than typical residential customers — cutting usage 7.6% for every 10% rate increase in the short run (elasticity of -0.76). About half of that response persists long-run (elasticity of -0.37), reflecting permanent crop-switching and fallowing rather than pure temporary conservation. That elasticity is the clearest evidence that ag electricity costs are already a load-bearing part of farm economics, not a rounding error.

sections.heading: PG&E Agricultural Rate Schedules: AG-A, AG-B, AG-C
sections.body:
PG&E ag customers sit on one of several time-of-use schedules, and the differences matter for how solar offsets your bill. AG-A-1/A-2 and AG-B are straight per-kWh time-of-use rates with no demand charge: summer (June-September) peak hours run 5pm-8pm daily. AG-B's summer peak generation rate is $0.22830/kWh, dropping to $0.11482 off-peak in summer and further to $0.08573 in winter off-peak. AG-A runs slightly lower across the board — $0.21359 summer peak down to $0.07579 winter off-peak.

AG-C adds a demand-charge component (a separate fee based on your peak kW draw, not just kWh consumed) in exchange for a flatter, somewhat lower per-kWh rate: $0.12733 summer peak, $0.09999 summer off-peak. That structure tends to suit operations with large, continuous pump draw rather than short sharp peaks.

One caveat that matters if you're comparing quotes: these figures are the generation charge only, from a Community Choice Aggregator's published comparison sheet dated February 15, 2026. PG&E's own delivery (transmission and distribution) charges, plus a PCIA "exit fee" that ranges from roughly -$0.0094/kWh (a credit, for newer-vintage accounts) to a small positive charge for older-vintage accounts, get added on top. Your all-in bundled rate will run higher than the generation numbers above — ask your PG&E rep or installer for your account's actual all-in ag rate before finalizing system size. A second caveat: we confirmed the source document exists at the cited URL with the stated February 15, 2026 effective date, but the PDF did not return machine-readable text in this correction pass, so the individual digits above were not independently re-verified against the source in this round — treat them as a starting point sourced from that document, not a substitute for pulling the actual rate sheet or asking PG&E directly before finalizing payback math. Older legacy schedules (AG-1, AG-4, AG-5, AG-R, AG-V) were phased out for new enrollment starting March 2021; if you're still on one, you're likely grandfathered and should not assume these current AG-A/B/C numbers apply to your bill.

sections.heading: SCE Agricultural and Pumping Rates: TOU-PA-2 and TOU-PA-3
sections.body:
SCE's agricultural and pumping schedules work on a different structure than PG&E's. TOU-PA-2 covers demand under 200 kW; TOU-PA-3 covers 200-500 kW, with special provisions above 500 kW for water agencies. To qualify, at least 70% of your electricity use has to go to agricultural power service, water or sewage pumping, or oil pumping — no meaningful domestic-purpose load allowed on the balance.

SCE gives ag and pumping customers two structural choices. Option D charges both a time-related demand charge (based on your peak-period draw) and a facilities-related demand charge (based on your monthly maximum demand regardless of time), in exchange for lower energy rates. Option E drops the time-related demand charge entirely in exchange for higher per-kWh energy rates — which tends to be the better fit once you add solar and battery storage, since it avoids penalizing whatever peak draw still happens after your system covers what it can.

Ag and pumping customers also get to choose their on-peak window: either the standard 4pm-9pm commercial window or a narrower 5pm-8pm ag-specific window. Winter includes a super-off-peak window from 8am-4pm weekdays — the cheapest power of the year, and it lines up almost exactly with when solar panels produce, which is the best midday offset opportunity on the whole rate structure.

We were not able to verify SCE's current cents-per-kWh figures for TOU-PA-2/TOU-PA-3 in this research — the fact sheet describing this structure carries a 2018 print code and no dollar figures, and SCE's tariff books returned unreadable formats on fetch. Don't quote a specific SCE ag rate as fact; pull the current tariff book at sce.com/tariffbooks or ask your account rep for the number before running payback math.

sections.heading: NEM Aggregation: One Array, Multiple Meters
sections.body:
Net Energy Metering Aggregation (NEMA), authorized by SB 594 in 2012, is the single most important mechanism on this page. It lets a customer-generator combine load from multiple meters — on properties they own, lease, or rent — as long as those parcels are attached, adjacent, or contiguous, with one solar system offsetting the combined total. The system is capped at 1 MW.

Without aggregation, a farm with a home meter and three separate irrigation pump meters would need to either pick one meter to serve (leaving the others on full retail rates) or build four separate small systems, each sized against a load profile that spikes for five months and sits flat the rest of the year — an expensive and inefficient way to build. With aggregation, all four meters count as one load, and the system gets sized against the combined annual profile, which is what makes the economics work at all for seasonal pumping. One trade-off worth knowing before you elect aggregation: doing so permanently forfeits eligibility for Net Surplus Compensation (NSC), the separate credit paid for surplus generation at year's end — not a decision to make lightly if your system is likely to run a large annual surplus.

Worth flagging, and now confirmed rather than hedged: AB 942 (2025-26), effective January 1, 2026, is narrower than early coverage of it suggested and does not broadly restructure net metering for existing NEM 1.0/2.0 customers. It applies specifically to a "new eligible customer-generator" — someone who buys property that already has a NEM 1.0/2.0 solar system installed on it — shifting that successor owner onto post-2022 compensation terms instead of letting them inherit the seller's legacy NEM deal. We pulled the bill text directly: it states, "This section does not apply to new eligible customer-generators that are public schools or agricultural customers" (Pub. Util. Code § 2827.2(d)). So if your farm buys land that already has a NEM 1.0/2.0 system on it, AB 942 does not force you onto worse terms — that exemption is confirmed against the statute, not just directionally likely.

sections.heading: USDA REAP Grants: Paused, Not Dead
sections.body:
This is the fact that changes the financing conversation for 2026. USDA announced on April 1, 2026 that it was rescinding the October 2024 REAP funding notice and halting new grant awards, to comply with Executive Order 14315, which targets what the order calls market-distorting subsidies for renewable energy. As of August 2026, USDA's own program page still showed grants not accepting applications, and nothing published since indicates a reopening date as of today.

Applicants who already submitted before the pause are expected to get a chance to reapply once new program rules are finalized, but USDA has given no timeline — the agency has called the new regulations "a top focus," which is not the same as a date. A new Notice of Funding Opportunity is expected to follow whenever those rules land.

What's still open: REAP guaranteed loans, processed year-round through local USDA Rural Development offices, unaffected by the grant pause.

On the caps that applied before the pause — solar projects capped at $1 million, energy-efficiency grants capped at $500,000, cost-share up to 25% under Farm Bill funding and up to 50% under now-expired IRA funding — treat these as last-known terms, not confirmed terms for whatever program eventually reopens. USDA Secretary Rollins has separately signaled intent to discourage ground-mounted solar on productive farmland, which could mean tighter eligibility or lower scoring for exactly the kind of ground-mount ag system this page discusses, once a new NOFO is published. Don't build a financing plan around REAP terms carrying forward unchanged.

sections.heading: What Farm-Scale Solar Actually Costs (and What We Don't Know Yet)
sections.body:
No primary source publishes a California price for a farm-scale ground-mount array. The closest primary figures are national: LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for small non-residential systems (100 kWdc or less) at $2.50 to $4.30 per watt and for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national. LBNL's large non-residential category includes ground-mounted systems, and farm arrays in the tens of kilowatts to megawatt range fall across both bands, so extrapolating from a residential rooftop quote to a 250 kW ground-mount system would be guessing dressed up as data.

Separately, if what you actually need is a dedicated solar-powered pump rather than a grid-tied array feeding your existing electric pump under NEM, that's a different product category with its own pricing; no primary source publishes it. Get a written, itemized quote from a CSLB-licensed installer sized against your actual acreage and load before budgeting off any number you find online.

sections.heading: SGMA, Fallowed Land, and the New Solar-on-Farmland Opening
sections.body:
The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act is reshaping Central Valley land use whether or not a given farm ever installs solar. Groundwater basins must hit sustainability targets by 2040 or 2042 depending on basin priority, and the Public Policy Institute of California estimates 500,000 to 900,000 acres of San Joaquin Valley farmland — roughly 10 to 20 percent of the valley's irrigated footprint — may need to come out of full irrigation to meet those targets, with the lower end assuming new water supplies materialize and the upper end assuming they don't.

That pressure is opening a real, if still-forming, path: converting land that has to come out of active irrigation anyway into solar generation instead of leaving it fallow and unproductive. Assembly Bill 1156 would help that transition along by eliminating Williamson Act contract-cancellation fees — normally 12.5% of unrestricted fair market value — for landowners converting dry or fallowed farmland to solar in SGMA-impacted Central Valley and Central Coast regions, and by converting contract cancellation from a permanent rescission into a temporary suspension so the land could theoretically return to farming later. It passed the state Senate 21-14 and, as of September 3, 2026, was reported awaiting the Governor's signature — not yet enacted law. If this matters to your land-use planning, confirm current signature status before treating it as available.

This is a land-use opportunity for acreage coming out of production, not an argument for putting solar on land you're still actively farming. If your fields are fully in production and staying that way, this section doesn't apply to you yet.

sections.heading: Batteries and Timing Under Ag Rate Schedules
sections.body:
The economics of adding battery storage to an ag solar system come down to matching your rate schedule's structure to your pump schedule. On PG&E's AG-A/AG-B/AG-C schedules, the 5pm-8pm peak window is exactly when a battery earns its keep — storing midday solar production and discharging it into the highest-priced hours instead of exporting it at low net-billing credit rates. On SCE's TOU-PA-2/3 schedules, choosing Option E (no time-related demand charge) removes the penalty for whatever peak draw remains after solar and battery cover what they can, which matters if your pumps sometimes have to run into the evening during peak irrigation weeks regardless of price.

One structural note that applies statewide, not just to ag accounts: publicly owned utilities — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, Turlock Irrigation District — are not subject to CPUC net billing rules at all and set their own export terms. If your operation is served by one of these rather than PG&E, SCE, or SDG&E, none of the NEM 3.0/net billing urgency in this page applies to you directly; check your own utility's ag rate schedule and export terms instead, since they can differ substantially from the investor-owned utility structures described above.

whenThisIsWrong: Solar doesn't pencil here if your pump load is small, isolated, and can't be aggregated — a single well meter on land you don't own the surrounding parcels of, running a few months a year, rarely generates enough offset to justify interconnection and system costs even with net metering. It's also the wrong move if your capital plan depended on a REAP grant landing this year: that funding is paused with no reopening date, not delayed by a few weeks, and building a proforma around a grant cost-share that may not exist is how projects stall mid-construction. If your fields are in full, ongoing production, the SGMA/AB 1156 fallowed-land angle doesn't apply to you — that's a story about land coming out of irrigation, not land staying in it. And if you're still on a legacy PG&E AG-1/AG-4/AG-5/AG-R/AG-V schedule, don't size a system against the current AG-A/AG-B/AG-C numbers in this page; your actual rate structure is different and needs its own pull from PG&E before you run payback math.

faqs.question: Is USDA REAP still accepting grant applications right now?
faqs.answer: No. USDA announced on April 1, 2026 that it was rescinding the October 2024 REAP funding notice and halting new grant awards, to comply with Executive Order 14315 targeting subsidies for solar and other renewable energy, and as of September 2026 no new Notice of Funding Opportunity has been published. Farmers who already submitted applications will reportedly get to reapply once new program rules are finalized, but USDA has given no completion date. The one piece of REAP that is NOT paused: guaranteed loans through local USDA Rural Development offices, which continue to be accepted year-round. If your financing plan depended on a REAP grant covering part of project cost, treat that funding as unavailable until further notice, not delayed.

faqs.question: What's the actual difference between PG&E's AG-A, AG-B, and AG-C rate schedules?
faqs.answer: AG-A and AG-B are straight time-of-use generation rates with no demand charge — you pay more per kWh during the 5-8pm peak window (summer AG-B peak is $0.22830/kWh) and less off-peak, with no penalty for how much power you draw at any one moment. AG-C adds a demand charge component on top of a flatter per-kWh rate, which suits operations with large, steady pump draw rather than short peak bursts. These are generation-only figures from PG&E's Feb 2026 rate sheet as published by a Community Choice Aggregator — delivery charges and PCIA are added on top of every schedule, so your actual bill runs higher than these numbers alone, and the individual digits should be confirmed against the source or PG&E directly before you rely on them.

faqs.question: Can one solar array offset several irrigation pump meters on my property?
faqs.answer: Yes, through Net Energy Metering Aggregation (NEMA), authorized by SB 594 (2012). If you own, lease, or rent the parcels and the meters sit on land that's attached, adjacent, or contiguous, one system up to 1 MW can be sized against the combined load of a home meter plus multiple pump meters. This is the mechanism that makes ag solar work at all for seasonal irrigation load — without it, you'd need a standalone system at every pump meter, and most individual pump meters don't run enough hours per year to pay one back. One trade-off: electing aggregation permanently forfeits eligibility for Net Surplus Compensation on any year-end surplus generation.

faqs.question: Does NEM 3.0 apply to my farm's pumps the same way it hits a homeowner's rooftop system?
faqs.answer: NEM 3.0 (net billing) governs PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E export compensation the same way for ag NEM-aggregation customers as for anyone else — there's no separate ag carve-out from net billing itself. Where ag customers do get a specific, confirmed exemption is under AB 942 (2025-26), effective January 1, 2026 — a narrower bill than early coverage suggested. AB 942 only affects a "new eligible customer-generator" who buys property that already has an existing NEM 1.0/2.0 system installed, shifting that successor owner onto post-2022 compensation terms. We pulled the bill text directly: "This section does not apply to new eligible customer-generators that are public schools or agricultural customers" (Pub. Util. Code § 2827.2(d)). So if your farm buys land with an existing NEM 1.0/2.0 system already on it, that specific successor-owner downgrade does not apply to you — confirmed against the statute.

faqs.question: What does AB 1156 do for farmland conversion to solar, and is it law yet?
faqs.answer: AB 1156 would eliminate Williamson Act contract-cancellation fees (normally 12.5% of unrestricted fair market value) for landowners converting fallowed or dry farmland to solar in SGMA-impacted Central Valley and Central Coast regions, and would convert contract cancellation from permanent to temporary suspension. It passed the state Senate 21-14. As of September 5, 2026, it was reported as awaiting the Governor's signature — not yet enacted. Confirm current status on the bill's leginfo.ca.gov page before treating this as available law for your project.

faqs.question: How much does a farm-scale solar system cost per watt in the Central Valley?
faqs.answer: No primary source publishes a figure for 100 kW-plus ground-mount systems specific to the Central Valley, and this page does not make one up. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for small non-residential systems (100 kWdc or less) at $2.50 to $4.30 per watt and for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national — national figures, and LBNL's large non-residential category includes ground-mount. Get a written quote from a CSLB-licensed installer sized to your actual load and acreage before budgeting off any per-watt figure you find online.

faqs.question: Are water district or irrigation district pumping arrangements different from a standard ag rate schedule?
faqs.answer: Often, yes — some irrigation districts operate under their own power arrangements or wholesale contracts rather than a standard utility ag tariff, and district-level incentive programs for pump electrification or solar do exist in some areas. We have not independently researched specific district programs for this page. If your pumping is billed through a water or irrigation district rather than directly by PG&E or SCE, ask your district for its own rate schedule and any solar or efficiency incentive it runs before assuming standard AG-A/AG-B/TOU-PA numbers apply.

bottomLine: The financing picture for California farm solar in 2026 is worse than it was in 2025, not better. REAP grants have been closed since April 1, 2026, with no reopening date, and guaranteed loans are the only USDA channel still open. Federal residential and commercial tax credit changes don't hit agricultural entities the same way rooftop homeowners feel them, but the loss of a grant cost-share is a real hole in the capital stack for any farm that was counting on one. Farm businesses can look to the §48E commercial credit, since the residential §25D credit does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025; a solar facility whose construction began after July 4, 2026 must be placed in service by December 31, 2027 to get it. Confirm eligibility with a tax professional before assuming 48E fills the REAP gap. What still works: PG&E and SCE both let you aggregate a single array across every meter you own or lease on contiguous land, which is the only way pump-season-only load ever pencils against a year-round bill, and agricultural customers are confirmed exempt from AB 942's narrower successor-owner NEM downgrade. SGMA-driven fallowing and AB 1156's Williamson Act fee waiver (once signed) point toward ground-mount on retired acreage as a live opportunity. Get your utility's exact ag rate sheet and a farm-scale contractor quote before running numbers — the generic residential $/watt figures floating around the internet don't apply to your acreage.

metaTitle: Church Solar Projects in California: Elective Pay vs PPA
metaDescription: How California church solar projects are owned, paid for and sized: IRS elective pay, developer PPAs, the 2027 federal deadline, net billing and property tax.
h1: Church Solar Projects in California: Elective Pay, PPAs and the 2027 Deadline
intro:
A California church can own its solar system and receive the federal clean electricity credit as a payment from the IRS, even though it owes no income tax. That is elective pay under 26 U.S.C. §6417, and it only works if the congregation owns the equipment. The other road is a lease or power purchase agreement, where a developer owns the system and keeps the credit. Every church solar project in the state is one of those two deals.

Timing now drives both. For a solar facility whose construction began after July 4, 2026, the federal credit does not apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2027. A building that sits mostly empty during the week and fills up on the weekend also sizes very differently from an office. This page works through ownership, the deadline, sizing under net billing, batteries, cost, property tax and what California church projects typically include. Statutes and program pages were checked September 23, 2026.

sections.heading: Own It or Lease It: The Fork Every Church Project Takes
sections.body:
Section 6417 lets an "applicable entity" elect to be treated as having paid tax equal to an applicable credit, which the IRS then pays out. The statute's list of applicable entities starts with "any organization exempt from the tax imposed by subtitle A," which covers a tax-exempt church, and it names the §48E clean electricity investment credit as an applicable credit.

The condition that decides everything is ownership. The IRS elective pay FAQ says that, apart from one manufacturing credit, "the applicable entity or electing taxpayer must both own the underlying eligible credit property and conduct the activities giving rise to the credit." If a developer owns the panels under a PPA or lease, the developer claims the credit and the congregation cannot. A lease is not a second route to the same payment.

So the choice is about capital and capacity, not about which deal "gets the credit." Owning means raising the full cost up front or borrowing it, handling IRS registration and a tax filing, and maintaining the equipment. Leasing means no capital outlay and no tax paperwork, in exchange for a long contract and a per-kWh or monthly price that may or may not pass much of the credit back to you.

sections.heading: How Elective Pay Works for a Congregation
sections.body:
The IRS describes a sequence that a finance committee should treat like a grant deadline. First, the system is placed in service; the IRS says pre-filing registration can be completed once you have all required information, including that placed-in-service date. Second, the church completes the IRS pre-filing registration, which the IRS calls "a required electronic process" for anyone making an elective payment election, and receives a registration number for the property.

Third, the election is made on a return. The FAQ says a tax-exempt organization that does not otherwise file a return uses Form 990-T, due on the organization's normal return due date, generally the 15th day of the fifth month after year end, with a six-month extension available. The IRS registration page asks filers to register "at least 120 days before the due date (including extensions) for the return where you report the credits." Build that 120 days into the calendar; waiting until the spring after installation is how a finished project misses its filing.

The church will also want a tax professional who has filed an elective pay return before. One statutory detail matters for larger campuses: for an elective pay claim on a facility of 1 MW AC or more whose construction began after December 31, 2025, §48E(d)(5) and §45Y(g)(12) reduce the credit to zero unless the domestic content requirement is met or a Treasury exception applies. A system under 1 MW AC is not reduced.

sections.heading: The Federal Deadline: What the Statute Says Now
sections.body:
Section 48E(e)(4) says the credit "shall not apply to any qualified property placed in service by the taxpayer after December 31, 2027, which is part of an applicable facility," meaning a wind or solar facility. The effective-date note from Public Law 119-21 applies that cutoff to facilities whose construction begins after July 4, 2026, twelve months after the law was enacted. As of September 23, 2026, a church that had not begun construction by July 4 must have its solar placed in service by December 31, 2027 to receive any credit.

What counted as beginning construction was set out in IRS Notice 2025-42, which required physical work of a significant nature and kept a 5% cost safe harbor only for solar facilities of 1.5 MW AC or less. On June 6, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia vacated that notice in full and remanded it to the IRS in Oregon Environmental Council v. Internal Revenue Service. If a congregation believes its project began construction before July 5, 2026, it should get a written position from a tax professional that accounts for the ruling and anything the IRS has issued since.

Two other statutory rules matter to church projects. For construction beginning after December 31, 2025, the credit is denied if the facility includes material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity; under §7701(a)(52), the required cost ratio is 40% for a solar facility beginning construction in 2026 and 45% in 2027. And an owner that is itself a specified foreign entity or foreign-influenced entity cannot claim the credit. Ask any installer how it documents the sourcing ratio, and who bears the loss if it fails.

sections.heading: If You Lease: Reading a Developer's PPA
sections.body:
A PPA or lease suits a congregation that lacks capital, does not want to carry equipment, or cannot take on the filing. A developer owns and maintains the system and sells the church electricity or charges a fixed payment. LBNL's 2026 data update found third-party ownership roughly twice as common at tax-exempt sites as at commercial ones in 2025, with the highest rates at "other" tax-exempt sites, many of them houses of worship. Leasing is the common path for churches, not the exception.

The risk is in the contract terms, not the concept. Read the starting rate and escalator against the church's own tariff over the whole term, the buyout dates and prices, what happens if the developer sells the project, who removes the system if the roof needs replacing, and what happens if the congregation sells or repurposes the property. Confirm the developer's own tax position too: a PPA priced on a credit the developer cannot get is a PPA that may be repriced or abandoned.

sections.heading: What California Church Solar Projects Look Like
sections.body:
Houses of worship are a visible share of the state's tax-exempt solar market. LBNL's Tracking the Sun 2024 summary says tax-exempt customers, including government, schools, religious and other nonprofits, made up 15% of U.S. non-residential installations in 2023. Its 2026 update puts roughly half of 2025 non-residential installs on commercial buildings, a third on agricultural land and the rest at tax-exempt sites.

A church campus usually offers three surfaces. The sanctuary roof is often steep, visible and architecturally sensitive. The fellowship hall, offices or school buildings tend to have simpler roofs. The parking lot can take a canopy, which adds structure cost but shades cars on hot Sundays. Many campuses also have several utility meters, one per building, so ask whether one array can serve several accounts under the utility's aggregation or virtual net billing rules before sizing each building separately.

New construction changes the question. The California Energy Commission's 2025 nonresidential solar guidance lists religious worship among the building types that Section 140.10(a) of the 2025 Energy Code requires to have solar PV when newly constructed, generally with battery storage unless an exception applies. A congregation building a new sanctuary or hall should plan for solar in the design, not as an add-on.

When you ask bidders for references, ask specifically for completed projects at other congregations with a similar roof and meter setup, and call them. Ask what the church's bill looked like in the first full year compared with the proposal.

sections.heading: Sizing for a Weekend Peak Under Net Billing
sections.body:
Since April 15, 2023, customers of PG&E, SCE and SDG&E who apply for interconnection take service on the CPUC's net billing tariff. The CPUC says export compensation reflects the value of that generation to the grid and "is usually lower than the retail rate," using values from its Avoided Cost Calculator.

That matters more for a church than for most buildings. Many congregations use little power Monday through Friday and a lot on the weekend. A system sized to cover the weekend peak will export most of its weekday output at those lower export values instead of offsetting power bought at retail. For most churches on an investor-owned utility, the better starting point is weekday baseline load, with the weekend covered partly by solar and partly by the grid or a battery.

Publicly owned utilities such as LADWP and SMUD are outside the CPUC tariff and set their own export terms, so a church served by one should get that utility's current rules before sizing.

sections.heading: Batteries: What the Statute Allows and Why SGIP Won't Help Now
sections.body:
The Self-Generation Incentive Program's own metrics page, checked September 23, 2026, showed the Large-Scale Storage budget closed at Step 5 ($0.25/Wh) and Non-Residential Storage Equity closed at Step 5 ($0.85/Wh) for PG&E, SCE, SoCalGas and the Center for Sustainable Energy. The categories still taking waitlist entries are residential equity budgets, which a church would not normally fit. Do not budget a storage project around an SGIP payment.

Federal treatment of storage differs from solar. Section 48E(e)(4)(C) excepts energy storage placed at a solar facility from the December 31, 2027 cutoff. Instead, storage follows the §48E(e) phase-out: using the "applicable year" of 2032 set in §45Y(d)(3), storage whose construction begins in 2033 keeps the full credit, 2034 gets 75%, 2035 gets 50%, and later starts get nothing. The prohibited-foreign-entity cost ratio for storage is stricter than for solar: 55% for construction beginning in 2026 and 60% in 2027 under §7701(a)(52). A church that owns a battery can take the storage credit through elective pay on the same terms as solar equipment, subject to the same ownership requirement.

A battery earns its keep by storing weekday solar for weekend use or by cutting demand charges. Get it priced as its own line, compare bids in dollars per usable kWh, and run the math on your own interval data.

sections.heading: Cost and Property Tax: The Two Numbers to Budget Against
sections.body:
No public source publishes a California church solar price. The closest primary figures are LBNL's. Its Tracking the Sun 2024 summary reports that large California systems (over 100 kW) at tax-exempt sites had a 2023 median price of $4.1 per watt, against $2.3 for commercial sites, and the full report lists domestic-content or prevailing-wage requirements, the prevalence of shade or parking structures, and lower borrowing costs as possible reasons. For smaller systems, the same summary reports state-level medians of $2.6 to $4.1 per watt for small non-residential systems. Use these to read a quote, not as a quote.

On property tax, most sanctuaries already use California's religious exemption. The Board of Equalization says it covers property owned by a religious organization and used exclusively for religious worship and school purposes, under Revenue and Taxation Code section 207, and it requires a claim filed with the county assessor. Separately, the new-construction exclusion for active solar energy systems in section 73 becomes inoperative on January 1, 2027; systems excluded before then remain excluded until the property changes ownership, according to BOE Letter to Assessors 2026/034. That matters for parts of a campus that are not exempt and for developer-owned equipment on church land, which may not share the church's exemption. Ask the county assessor before signing a PPA.

It is also the wrong plan if the system cannot realistically be placed in service by December 31, 2027 and the project did not begin construction by July 4, 2026, because the solar credit is then zero. A PPA is the wrong move if the church may sell, subdivide or rebuild within the contract term without a clear buyout. And no statement on this page is tax advice: have a tax professional review the ownership structure, the construction-start facts and the sourcing documents before anyone signs.

faqs.question: Can a church get a cash payment from the IRS for solar?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the church owns the system. Under 26 U.S.C. §6417, a tax-exempt organization is an applicable entity that can elect to receive the §48E credit as a payment. The IRS says the entity must own the property, register before filing (at least 120 days before the return due date, including extensions) and make the election on a return such as Form 990-T.

faqs.question: What's the difference between elective pay and a PPA for a church?
faqs.answer: Ownership. Elective pay requires the church to own the equipment. Under a PPA or lease, the developer owns the system and claims the credit. A church cannot combine the two on the same equipment.

faqs.question: Is the 2027 deadline real?
faqs.answer: Yes. Section 48E(e)(4) ends the credit for solar property placed in service after December 31, 2027 when the facility's construction began after July 4, 2026. For a project that has not started, the calendar from contract to utility permission to operate is the constraint.

faqs.question: Does the small-project safe harbor still apply to a church system?
faqs.answer: It is unsettled. IRS Notice 2025-42 limited the 5% cost safe harbor to solar facilities of 1.5 MW AC or less, and a federal district court vacated that notice in full on June 6, 2026. Get a written position from a tax professional before relying on any construction-start method.

faqs.question: Is there a battery rebate for churches?
faqs.answer: Not from SGIP right now. Its non-residential storage budgets showed closed for all four program administrators on September 23, 2026. A church that owns a battery can use elective pay for the storage credit, which follows its own phase-out schedule in §48E(e).

faqs.question: What do California church solar projects usually include?
faqs.answer: A roof array on the sanctuary or hall, sometimes a parking canopy, and often several meters across the campus. New churches built under the 2025 Energy Code generally have to include solar, because the CEC lists religious worship among the building types covered by Section 140.10(a).

faqs.question: Will solar trigger a property tax reassessment on church property?
faqs.answer: Property used exclusively for religious worship can be exempt under the religious exemption, which requires a claim with the county assessor. The separate solar new-construction exclusion becomes inoperative on January 1, 2027. Developer-owned equipment may be treated differently, so ask the assessor before signing a PPA.

bottomLine: A California church choosing solar in late 2026 is choosing between two deals: own the system and receive the §48E credit as an IRS payment under §6417, or let a developer own it under a PPA or lease and keep the credit. The calendar sits on top of both. Solar that began construction after July 4, 2026 has to be placed in service by December 31, 2027 to earn any credit, and the construction-start rules are in flux after a June 2026 court ruling. Size for weekday load, not the weekend peak, because net billing pays less for exports than the retail rate. Do not count on an SGIP battery payment. Get bids that separate each piece of the scope, check the contractor's CSLB license, and have a tax professional who has filed an elective pay return review the plan. California Rate Relief doesn't install systems or hold a contractor's license; it forwards commercial inquiries to an independent provider, subject to service availability.

metaTitle: Commercial Battery Storage California: 2026 Costs & ROI
metaDescription: Commercial battery storage in California, 2026: SGIP's commercial storage category is closed, the 48E credit drives the math, and demand charges decide payback.
h1: Commercial Battery Storage in California: Demand Charges, Costs, and the 2026 Incentive Picture
intro:
The CPUC's program page lists SGIP's Large-Scale Storage funding as available through 2025, and the program administrators' tracker shows the category closed for every administrator (selfgenca.com, as of September 22, 2026). If a vendor's proposal to you still includes an SGIP rebate line item, that line item is wrong, and you should ask why it's there.

That single fact reframes the whole conversation. For years, the SGIP rebate — up to $0.25 per watt-hour before it was reduced for projects also taking the federal tax credit — was baked into every commercial battery pitch in the state. It's gone for new general-market applicants. What's left is a smaller number of levers, and they matter more now that one of them disappeared: the 30% federal Section 48E investment tax credit, and the demand charges on your actual utility bill.

This page is not about backup power. For a commercial or industrial account, backup is a nice side effect of owning a battery, not the reason to buy one. The reason to buy one is demand charges — the part of your bill based on your single highest 15-minute power draw each month, not how much energy you used — which can be a large share of a California C&I customer's bill; your own bill shows how large. A battery that shaves that peak down is the entire business case. Everything below is built around that math, what drives the cost, and where it doesn't work.

sections.heading: SGIP is closed. Plan around that, not around a reopening.
sections.body:
The Self-Generation Incentive Program's Large-Scale Storage category — the non-residential bucket that funded most commercial battery projects in California for a decade — is closed to new applicants. SelfGenCA's program metrics page shows it at Step 5 with status "Closed" for CSE, SCE, SoCalGas and PG&E as of September 22, 2026, and the CPUC's program page lists Large-Scale Storage funding as "available through 2025." The Non-Residential Storage Equity category also shows closed. The only residential category with a waitlist is the income-qualified Residential Solar and Storage Equity program under AB 209 — residential-only, irrelevant to a commercial project.

As of this writing, no CPUC decision or legislative action has authorized a fresh round of general-market commercial storage funding that this page could find. That could change, but nothing in the record supports promising a reopening date to a client, and neither should a vendor's proposal. The Step 5 rate is listed at $0.25/Wh standard, or $0.18/Wh for projects also taking the federal investment tax credit — cite that as history, not as money you can still get.

sections.heading: What actually pays for the battery: demand charges, not backup
sections.body:
Most commercial electric bills have two components: a volumetric energy charge (cents per kWh consumed) and a demand charge (dollars per kW based on your single highest sustained draw in the billing period, usually measured over a 15-minute window). Demand charges are disconnected from total energy use — a facility that runs lean most of the month but spikes hard for twenty minutes during a shift change or equipment startup can carry a demand charge as large as its entire energy bill.

Demand charges can be a large share of a California commercial or industrial customer's total electric bill; the demand line on your own bill tells you how large. A battery that discharges during that peak window and recharges when the facility's draw is low doesn't need to store much energy relative to the facility's total consumption; it needs to be sized to the gap between peak and average demand, which is why demand-charge management is a fundamentally different sizing exercise than backup power or solar self-consumption.

This is also why backup power is the wrong frame for evaluating one of these systems. A battery sized to ride out a demand spike for 15-60 minutes a few times a month is not sized to keep a building running through a multi-hour outage, and a battery sized for meaningful backup duration is usually oversized and uneconomical for demand-charge work alone. Decide which problem you're solving before a vendor sizes the system for you.

sections.heading: The peak-shaving math, worked through
sections.body:
There's no way to give a single California-wide demand-charge number that means anything, because PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E each publish their own commercial tariffs with different rate structures, and the current tariff sheets for PG&E's B-19/B-20 and SDG&E's AL-TOU commercial schedules were not obtainable in readable form for this page — that number needs to come from your actual bill or a fresh tariff pull, not a blog average. One hard data point exists in the record: SCE's TOU-GS-3, Option R facilities-related demand charge was $18.71/kW per month as of a mid-2022 tariff filing. SCE restructured its commercial time-of-use windows in a 2024-2025 rate case, so treat that figure as historical context, not a number to plug into a 2026 proposal without verifying against a current tariff sheet.

The calculation method matters more than any single rate. Take a generic illustrative example (not a California-specific rate): a facility peaking at 1,200 kW that shaves 30% off its peak, down to 840 kW, at an example demand rate of $15/kW, cuts its monthly demand charge from $18,000 to $12,600 — a savings of $5,400 a month, or $64,800 a year. Run that same formula with your actual utility's demand rate and your actual peak-reduction target, and you have a real number instead of a marketing one.

Vendor case studies report peak reductions and savings for named customers; those are the vendor's own claims, so ask any vendor for the interval data behind a case study before treating its percentages as a guide to your site.

sections.heading: What a system actually costs
sections.body:
No primary source publishes a California installed price for commercial battery storage, and the blog and vendor ranges that circulate online are not a basis for a budget. The price depends on usable capacity, power rating, the inverter and switchgear work, the site and the integrator. Ask each bidder for the installed price, the usable kWh and the continuous kW, and compare bids in dollars per usable kWh.

Residential battery prices are not a substitute for a commercial quote. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) estimates that storage added roughly $750 to $1,000 per kWh to the price of paired residential systems in 2023, nationally; commercial systems are larger and priced differently, so use that only to recognize a quote that looks out of line.

sections.heading: The federal 48E credit is the incentive that matters now
sections.body:
With SGIP closed to new commercial applicants, the federal Section 48E investment tax credit is the primary incentive lever left standing, and it's arguably a stronger one than SGIP ever was for storage specifically. Energy storage technology qualifies for §48E on its own. The rate is 30% for storage with a capacity under 1 MW or meeting the prevailing-wage and apprenticeship rules (6% otherwise), and the statute phases the credit out by construction-start year: with the applicable year fixed at 2032 by §45Y(d)(3), storage whose construction begins in 2033 keeps 100% of the credit, 2034 starts get 75%, 2035 starts get 50%, and later starts get nothing. Unlike the residential 25D credit, which expired for good on December 31, 2025, 48E does not require the storage to be paired with solar — a storage-only commercial project qualifies on its own.

There's a compliance wrinkle worth knowing before you sign a contract: Foreign Entity of Concern ("FEOC") material-assistance rules require a minimum non-restricted-source cost share for the credit to apply — at least 55% for projects beginning construction in 2026, rising to 60% in 2027 and eventually 75% for projects starting in 2030 or later. A project that can't document its sourcing cost ratio risks losing the credit entirely. Ask your integrator directly how they document FEOC compliance before you sign anything.

The prohibited-foreign-entity rules apply to storage whose construction begins after December 31, 2025, under §48E(c)(3). On depreciation, §168(e)(3)(B)(viii) classifies energy storage technology as 5-year property, §168(k) provides a 100% first-year allowance for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025, and §50(c)(3) reduces the basis by half the credit; have a tax professional confirm how these apply before they go into a return model.

sections.heading: Sizing: follow the load, not the solar array
sections.body:
There is no verified industry-standard ratio for sizing battery capacity as a percentage of solar array size in California commercial projects, and any page that gives you one is making it up. The defensible engineering principle, repeated across multiple sources, is that storage should be sized to the gap between a facility's peak demand and its average or baseline demand — not to the size of a co-located solar system. A facility with a flat, steady load profile and no sharp demand spikes gets weak peak-shaving economics from a battery no matter how large the adjacent solar array is, because there's no meaningful peak to shave.

The one concrete sizing data point available — Stem's 350 kW / 800 kWh Penske deployment, roughly a 2.3-hour discharge duration — is consistent with what's commonly understood as typical for pure demand-charge management: short-to-medium duration systems, generally in the 2-4 hour range, sized to cover the peak window rather than to run a facility for an extended outage. A widely cited industry convention holds to a minimum roughly 2-hour discharge duration for projects seeking utility incentive programs, though that specific figure reflects general industry practice rather than something independently confirmed in current program rules for this page, and should be treated as background rather than a hard requirement.

Before sizing anything, pull twelve months of interval (15-minute) demand data from your utility account. If your monthly demand profile is flat, a battery is very likely the wrong tool for your building regardless of what a proposal says.

sections.heading: Vendors: what they actually do, and what they don't
sections.body:
Tesla's Megapack and Powerpack lines are proven at scale, but one industry-trend source characterizes them as optimized primarily for utility-scale deployment rather than commercial-and-industrial-specific projects — worth knowing so you don't assume Tesla is the default option for a mid-size commercial demand-charge project the way it might be for a utility-scale asset. (Arevon Energy's Nighthawk project — 329 Megapack units, 300 MW/1,200 MWh, commercial operation beginning August 2026 — is real, but it's a utility-scale asset, not a commercial-building case study, and shouldn't be cited as one.)

Fluence's Mosaic platform and Tesla's Autobidder are asset-management software layers for dispatch optimization and market bidding — relevant to understanding how a battery decides when to discharge, but they are software, not hardware vendors in the behind-the-meter commercial sense.

Stem Inc. is the most directly relevant name for demand-charge management specifically, with its Athena AI dispatch software paired to battery hardware and a real California track record (the LA-area Electrodes portfolio, the Penske deployment above). One flag worth passing to a client: industry trade coverage has reported Stem publicly pivoting from owning battery hardware toward a software-and-services model, which may matter for how a specific deal is structured — ask directly whether you'd be buying hardware from Stem or licensing dispatch software on top of someone else's battery.

Generac's Concerto and PWRcell lines serve smaller commercial accounts, and BYD and CATL are commonly referenced as cell suppliers integrated into other vendors' systems. No verifiable California-specific deployment data or current pricing was found for either in the research behind this page — mention them as market participants, not as a ranked recommendation. No vendor comparison table exists in the record; a defensible one would require direct RFP responses or spec-sheet pulls this page doesn't have.

whenThisIsWrong:
A flat-load facility — steady draw around the clock with no sharp demand spikes — gets weak peak-shaving economics from a battery no matter how the rest of the math looks. Pull twelve months of 15-minute interval data before assuming otherwise.

A business with modest demand-charge exposure rarely clears a battery's installed cost even after the 30% federal credit; the monthly savings don't outrun the capital.

Customers of publicly owned utilities — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, Turlock Irrigation District — are not subject to CPUC rules or NEM 3.0, and their demand-charge structures and available programs differ from PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E. Don't let anyone apply IOU urgency or IOU numbers to a publicly owned utility account.

Anyone counting on an SGIP rebate as part of the financial model is working from stale numbers — the commercial storage categories show closed on the SGIP tracker (as of September 22, 2026). And a project using battery cells that can't document a Foreign Entity of Concern-compliant cost ratio risks losing the 30% federal credit outright, which changes the payback math substantially. If a vendor promises a guaranteed payback without showing the demand-charge calculation behind it, that's a claim to verify, not a number to bank on.

faqs.question: Is SGIP still available for commercial battery storage in California?
faqs.answer: Not for new applicants, as of September 22, 2026. SelfGenCA's program metrics page shows the Large-Scale Storage category (the non-residential bucket) at Step 5, marked "Closed" for every administrator, and the CPUC's program page lists Large-Scale Storage funding as available through 2025. No reopening has been announced that this page could find, and none should be assumed or promised.

faqs.question: What's the actual federal tax credit for a commercial battery now?
faqs.answer: The Section 48E credit: 30% for storage under 1 MW or meeting the wage and apprenticeship rules, with the full credit for construction beginning through 2033, 75% of it for 2034 starts and 50% for 2035 starts. Unlike the residential solar credit that expired December 31, 2025, 48E doesn't require the battery to be paired with solar — a standalone commercial storage project qualifies on its own. There's a sourcing-compliance rule (Foreign Entity of Concern cost-ratio requirements) that can disqualify a project whose sourcing cost ratio isn't documented, so ask your integrator how they document it.

faqs.question: How much does a commercial battery system cost installed in California?
faqs.answer: No primary source publishes a California installed price for commercial battery storage, and the blog and vendor ranges that circulate online are not a basis for a budget. Ask each bidder for the installed price, usable kWh and continuous kW, compare bids in dollars per usable kWh, and get an actual bid before committing.

faqs.question: How is payback calculated without SGIP in the picture?
faqs.answer: Take your utility's actual demand charge rate in dollars per kW, multiply by the kW you expect to shave off your monthly peak, multiply by 12 months, then divide the installed cost (net of the 30% federal credit) by that annual savings figure. No primary source publishes a typical payback period, and marketing figures often assumed SGIP funding that is closed for new projects. Ask the vendor to show the calculation, not just the final number.

faqs.question: Does a commercial battery need solar to make financial sense?
faqs.answer: No. Storage sizing should follow the gap between your facility's peak demand and its average demand, not the size of a co-located solar array. A flat-load building gets poor economics from a battery regardless of solar, and the 48E federal credit applies to standalone storage without requiring a solar pairing. Solar and storage can work well together, but treat them as two separate financial decisions, not one bundled pitch.

faqs.question: Which vendors actually serve California commercial demand-charge projects?
faqs.answer: Stem Inc. has the most direct California C&I track record for demand-charge-specific work (its Athena software platform, a documented Los Angeles-area portfolio, and a named Penske Truck Leasing deployment), though trade coverage indicates Stem is shifting toward a software-and-services model rather than owning hardware outright — worth clarifying in any proposal. Tesla's Megapack/Powerpack line is proven but leans utility-scale. Generac serves smaller commercial accounts. No independently verified vendor pricing comparison exists as of this writing.

faqs.question: Do publicly owned utilities like LADWP or SMUD change this math?
faqs.answer: Yes, substantially. Publicly owned utilities — LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, Turlock Irrigation District among them — are not regulated by the CPUC and are not subject to NEM 3.0 or investor-owned-utility rate structures. metaDescription: What a 100 kW commercial solar system costs in California in 2026, using LBNL and NREL benchmarks. Cost drivers, the ITC deadline, and how to check payback.
h1: What a 100 kW Commercial Solar System Costs in California (2026)
intro:
No primary source publishes a California price for a 100 kW commercial system. The closest benchmarks are national. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for small non-residential systems (100 kWdc or less) at $2.50 to $4.30 per watt and for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national. A 100 kW system sits right at the line between those two bands, which puts it anywhere from about $170,000 to $430,000 before any tax credit, and site conditions decide where: composition roof versus tile, existing electrical service versus a costly service upgrade, straightforward permitting versus a full utility interconnection study.

The federal 30% investment tax credit under Section 48E is still available for a system this size, and 100 kW falls well under the 1 MW AC threshold that would otherwise require prevailing-wage and apprenticeship paperwork to hit the full rate. But the credit now comes with a hard deadline. Projects that haven't already begun construction have to be fully placed in service by December 31, 2027, or the credit drops to zero. That's roughly 15 months from today.

Meanwhile the program that used to help pay for a battery to offset demand charges, SGIP, is closed to new commercial applicants. This page covers the published cost benchmarks, where the money goes, how to estimate what 100 kW produces at your address, and how to check payback under the rules that apply right now.

sections.heading: The Real Cost Per Watt
sections.body:
NREL's last commercial rooftop benchmark, a 200 kWdc system modeled in Q1 2022, came in at a modeled market price of $1.84 per watt (2021 dollars, national average). NREL notes that actual costs vary significantly by region and installer, and a 2022 model is dated.

The more recent primary figures are LBNL's reported prices for systems installed in 2023. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for small non-residential systems (100 kWdc or less) at $2.50 to $4.30 per watt and for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national. A 100 kW rooftop job sits right at the boundary between those bands, so its price can fall in either. Composition or membrane roofs with adequate existing electrical service land toward the bottom. Tile roofs, standing-seam metal, older switchgear that needs a service upgrade, or a utility that requires a full interconnection study push the number toward the top. Get at least three itemized bids and compare them against these bands rather than against a single rule-of-thumb figure.

sections.heading: Where the Money Actually Goes
sections.body:
Hardware is not the majority of the invoice. NREL's commercial benchmark builds its price from module and inverter costs, structural and electrical balance-of-system, installation labor, sales tax, permitting, inspection and interconnection, EPC and developer overhead, contingency and profit — and the categories other than modules and inverters make up most of it. In plain terms: on a commercial rooftop system, engineering, permitting, interconnection and margin cost about as much as the equipment, or more.

That's worth knowing when a quote looks high on a per-watt basis relative to a residential job. It generally isn't hardware markup; it's the fixed cost of engineering, permitting, and interconnecting a commercial-scale system. Ask any installer quoting a 100 kW job for an itemized breakdown along those lines. If they can't produce one, that's a flag on its own.

sections.heading: The Tax Credit Deadline That Actually Matters Now
sections.body:
Section 48E pays 30% of the qualified investment for a facility with a maximum net output under 1 MW AC, and 100 kW is comfortably under that line. Below that line the 30% rate does not depend on the prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements, per 26 U.S.C. §48E(a)(2).

What changed is the deadline. The cutoff comes from the statute: §48E(e)(4) ends the credit for solar property placed in service after December 31, 2027, and Public Law 119-21 (signed July 4, 2025) applies that rule to facilities whose construction begins after July 4, 2026, twelve months after enactment. Projects that began construction by that date are outside the December 31, 2027 cutoff. For any project not yet underway, the system has to be placed in service by December 31, 2027 or the credit is zero; ask a tax professional what placed-in-service evidence you will need. That leaves roughly 15 to 16 months from today to design, permit, interconnect, and commission a system.

IRS Notice 2025-42 had let a solar facility of 1.5 MW AC or less, such as a 100 kW system, show that construction began either through physical work of a significant nature or through a 5% cost safe harbor; the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia vacated that notice in full on June 6, 2026, so ask a tax professional which method applies to your facts. For a project starting today with no cost yet incurred, the number that matters is the placed-in-service deadline, not the safe harbor. Under 26 U.S.C. §168(e)(3)(B)(viii), §48E qualified property and energy storage technology are 5-year property, and §168(k) provides a 100% first-year allowance for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025. Under §50(c)(3), the depreciable basis is reduced by half of the credit, leaving about 85% of the qualified cost depreciable when the credit is 30%. Get the exact interaction of the credit, the basis reduction, and any state-level depreciation treatment confirmed by a CPA before it goes into a payback model.

sections.heading: Annual Production: What 100 kW Actually Generates
sections.body:
No primary source publishes a single production figure for a 100 kW system in California; output depends on tilt, azimuth, shading and local weather. Coastal and fog-belt locations produce less than Central Valley and desert Southern California locations, which get higher irradiance and fewer overcast days.

Before signing a contract, run the address through NREL's PVWatts calculator (pvwatts.nrel.gov), which accounts for actual tilt, azimuth, shading, and local weather data. Any proposal for a system this size should include a PVWatts-derived, or equivalent, production estimate with the specific assumptions shown, not just an annual kWh number with no methodology behind it. If a proposal only gives a single number and no assumptions, ask for the modeling.

sections.heading: Demand Charges: Why Solar Alone Won't Fix Them
sections.body:
Demand charges are set in each utility's commercial tariff, and this page does not repeat the secondary, installer-blog figures that circulate for them. Pull the current B-19/B-20, TOU-8, or AL-TOU rate sheets directly from pge.com, sce.com, or sdge.com before building a payback model that leans on a specific demand-charge figure.

The mechanism matters more than the exact dollar figure: fully offsetting demand charges usually requires a battery timed to discharge during the peak window, not just solar generation. And the program that used to subsidize commercial batteries for exactly this purpose, SGIP, is not currently funding new applicants. As of September 22, 2026, both non-residential SGIP storage categories, Large-Scale Storage and Non-Residential Storage Equity, show closed at Step 5, at listed rates of $0.25/Wh and $0.85/Wh respectively. That means a battery sized to chase demand-charge savings is currently a fully out-of-pocket cost on top of the ITC-eligible solar system, not a subsidized add-on.

sections.heading: Net Billing: What You Get for Exported Power
sections.body:
California's commercial customers at PG&E, SCE, and SDG&E sit on the CPUC's Net Billing Tariff, the successor to net metering that most people still call NEM 3.0 even though that name technically describes the residential version. Export compensation is based on avoided cost rather than the retail rate you pay to buy power, and the CPUC says it is usually lower than the retail rate, though it can rise above it on late summer evenings. This is standard CPUC policy, laid out on the commission's own Net Energy Metering and Net Billing program page, and it applies to commercial and residential customers alike at all three utilities.

The practical upshot: a 100 kW system sized to export a large surplus back to the grid usually earns less for that power than it is worth used on-site. Right-sizing the system to your actual daytime load, rather than maximizing kW to fit the roof, usually produces a better payback than over-building and relying on export credits.

sections.heading: How to Check Payback Under Current Rules
sections.body:
Run the numbers straight, on your own quote. Start with the installed price. The 30% Section 48E credit comes off that price for a system under 1 MW AC, so a bid of $250,000, for example, would carry a $75,000 credit. That's the ITC in isolation. Some installers quote lower net-cost figures by also stacking the 100% bonus depreciation benefit described above on top of the credit; the value of that depends entirely on the buyer's marginal tax rate and isn't a figure that applies the same way to every business. Don't take a stacked net-cost number at face value. Ask the installer to itemize exactly which incentives and depreciation elections produce it, and confirm the depreciation math with your own CPA.

For the energy side, multiply the PVWatts production estimate for your address by the share you will use on-site and your tariff's energy prices, and value exports at the export credits instead. Divide the net cost by that yearly value for a simple payback. No primary source publishes a typical payback period for a 100 kW system, and demand-charge-heavy load profiles change the answer unless the system is paired with a battery, which, per the SGIP closure above, currently carries no rebate. The binding constraint for anyone starting today is the calendar: construction has to finish and the system has to be placed in service by December 31, 2027, to keep the 30% credit at all.

sections.heading: Vet the Contractor Like It's a Six-Figure Bet, Because It Is
sections.body: California's residential solar dealer network has taken serious hits. Freedom Forever filed Chapter 11 in April 2026 and was converted to Chapter 7 liquidation by court order on August 7, 2026, leaving its homeowners with no operating company behind their systems. Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025; Solaris Assets completed an acquisition of its assets and servicing platform that September, and SunStrong Management now runs day-to-day operations on the legacy portfolio. Neither entity is originating new agreements. SunPower filed Chapter 11 in August 2024. All three were primarily residential, dealer-network businesses, so their direct relevance to a commercial 100 kW EPC contract is lower, but the underlying lesson applies at least as hard on a six-figure commercial job: verify the contractor's CSLB license class and standing directly at cslb.ca.gov, confirm bonding, and ask how long they've operated as a commercial EPC specifically, not just how long the parent brand has existed. A firm that can't produce a current CSLB license number and a bond certificate on request shouldn't get anywhere near a six-figure contract, commercial or residential.

whenThisIsWrong: Skip this, or slow down, if any of these apply. Your business is served by a publicly owned utility (LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, Turlock Irrigation District) which set their own rates and terms; NEM 3.0 urgency doesn't apply there, so run the math on that utility's own tariff. Your load is dominated by demand charges rather than kWh usage, and you can't currently absorb an unsubsidized battery to address them, since SGIP is closed for commercial as of this writing. You're leasing the building and won't hold it past the payback window. The roof needs replacement soon. You have no tax appetite to use a 30% credit, as with nonprofits, government entities, or businesses with minimal tax liability. Or you can't realistically get a system designed, permitted, and placed in service by December 31, 2027.

faqs.answer: No primary source publishes a California price at exactly this size. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for small non-residential systems (100 kWdc or less) at $2.50 to $4.30 per watt and for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national, which puts a 100 kW system anywhere from about $170,000 to $430,000 before incentives. faqs.question: Is the federal solar tax credit still available for commercial systems?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Section 48E investment tax credit still pays 30% for systems under 1 MW AC, which covers a 100 kW system with room to spare, and systems that size don't need prevailing-wage documentation to get the full rate. The catch is timing: under §48E(e)(4), any project that hasn't already started construction, which as of today is most projects still being planned, must be fully placed in service by December 31, 2027, or the credit is zero. That's roughly 15 to 16 months from today.

faqs.question: Will solar reduce my demand charges?
faqs.answer: Only partially, and often not much on its own. Solar cuts the per-kWh part of your bill well but does little for demand charges, since commercial peak demand often occurs in late afternoon or evening as solar output is dropping. Fully addressing demand charges usually requires a battery discharging on a schedule timed to your peak, and the program that used to subsidize commercial batteries for this, SGIP, has both its non-residential budgets closed to new applicants as of September 2026. Budget for a battery as a fully unsubsidized cost right now.

faqs.question: How much electricity will a 100 kW system produce per year in California?
faqs.answer: It depends on the address, tilt, azimuth and shading: coastal fog-belt areas like San Francisco or coastal Los Angeles produce less than the Central Valley or desert Southern California. No primary source publishes a single California figure, so before signing anything, get a PVWatts-based (pvwatts.nrel.gov) or equivalent production estimate for your exact address, tilt, and shading, and ask your installer to show the assumptions behind whatever number they quote.

faqs.question: Can I still get an SGIP rebate for a battery paired with my system?
faqs.answer: No, not currently. As of September 22, 2026, both of SGIP's non-residential storage categories, Large-Scale Storage and Non-Residential Storage Equity, show closed at Step 5 for every program administrator, at listed rates of $0.25/Wh and $0.85/Wh respectively. There's no open commercial storage incentive path right now. If you need rebate-reopening timing, contact your utility's SGIP desk directly (PG&E: selfgen@pge.com; SCE: SGIPGroup@sce.com; CSE: sgip@energycenter.org) rather than assuming a rebate is baked into an installer's quote.

faqs.question: Does NEM 3.0 apply to my business if I'm on a public utility like LADWP or SMUD?
faqs.answer: No. Publicly owned utilities, including LADWP, SMUD, MID, Anaheim, Roseville, Lodi, Imperial Irrigation District, and Turlock Irrigation District, are not regulated by the CPUC and are not subject to NEM 3.0 or the Net Billing Tariff. They set their own net-metering and export terms. Don't let anyone apply NEM 3.0 urgency or CPUC export-rate assumptions to a project served by one of these utilities; check that utility's own current tariff instead.

faqs.question: How do I vet a commercial solar contractor given recent industry bankruptcies?
faqs.answer: Freedom Forever converted to Chapter 7 liquidation on August 7, 2026, after a Chapter 11 filing in April 2026, affecting its homeowners. Sunnova (Chapter 11, June 2025; assets acquired by Solaris Assets that September, with SunStrong Management now servicing the legacy portfolio) and SunPower (Chapter 11, August 2024) also failed, though all three were mainly residential dealer-network businesses. For a six-figure commercial contract, verify the contractor's CSLB license class and bond status directly at cslb.ca.gov, and ask specifically how long they've operated as a commercial EPC, not just how long the company brand has existed.

The 30% Section 48E credit is still available and doesn't depend on prevailing-wage compliance at this size, and it can be paired with the 100% first-year allowance §168(k) provides for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025. But any project not already under construction must be placed in service by December 31, 2027 to keep the credit at all. SGIP's commercial storage categories are closed, so a battery to chase demand-charge savings is now a fully unsubsidized cost. Confirm production with PVWatts and demand charges with your utility's current tariff sheet before signing anything. Vet any contractor's CSLB license and bond status before committing to them. California Rate Relief doesn't install systems or hold a contractor's license; it forwards commercial inquiries to an independent provider, subject to service availability.

metaDescription: What a 1 MW commercial solar system costs in California, using LBNL's benchmark, and what the 48E tax credit, interconnection, and financing actually require.
h1: What a 1 MW Commercial Solar System Costs in California in 2026
intro:
No primary source publishes a California price for a 1 MW commercial system. LBNL's Tracking the Sun (2024 Edition) put 2023 installed prices for large non-residential systems (over 100 kWdc) at $1.70 to $3.10 per watt, 20th to 80th percentile, national, which puts a 1 MW system at roughly $1.7 million to $3.1 million before any tax credit. That's the headline. It is not the number that decides whether the project makes sense.

The number that decides it is 1 MW itself. Under the federal §48E credit, a facility whose maximum net output is 1 megawatt AC or more gets the 30% rate only if it meets the prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements; otherwise the rate is the 6% base. A facility under 1 MW AC is automatically exempt from that requirement and gets 30% regardless. A 1 MW commercial system sits directly on that line, and the answer depends on how the project is sized and measured, not just its label.

Layer onto that a federal construction-start deadline that already passed as of today, an interconnection process that won't fast-track a system this size, and a state battery incentive that's technically closed in every California utility territory right now. This page walks through what's actually true, with sources, as of September 5, 2026.
